examples.note: Glory is what is given; God is who it goes to.

cards.name: Place
cards.eli5: Where it literally is. “Sitting in a circle.”

formula.note: A real spot you could point at.

cards.oneLine: The literal physical location.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — H: here, a real spot.
cards.mnemonicWhy: If you could stand there, it is place. If you could not, it is sphere.
cards.spotIt: Ask: could I actually point at this location?
cards.bookDef: Pinpoints the literal physical location of a noun in the dative case.

examples.english: those sitting *in a circle* around him
examples.note: A real ring of people on real ground.

cards.name: Sphere
cards.eli5: Where it is, but not really. “Sighing deeply in his spirit” — you cannot point at that.
cards.gist: In a realm, not a spot

formula.note: A place you cannot point at.

cards.oneLine: The figurative realm the action happens in.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — I: in what realm.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Place is a spot on a map. Sphere is a spot you can only imagine — in the spirit, in the flesh, in Christ.
cards.spotIt: It reads like a location, but nobody could stand there.
cards.bookDef: Identifies the figurative or metaphorical location (i.e., sphere or realm) of a noun in the dative case.
cards.watchOut: Place and sphere are one word doing literal and figurative duty. The test is whether you could point at it.

examples.note: A realm, not a room.

cards.name: Time
cards.eli5: When it happened. “On the third day.”

formula.note: A point in time, not a stretch.

cards.oneLine: The point in time at which it happened.
cards.mnemonic: HIT — T: then.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Location again, but on a calendar instead of a map. A moment, not a duration.
cards.spotIt: Ask: when? And check it is a moment rather than a length of time.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the point in time (location in time) at which the action of a verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: The accusative measures how long something went on. The dative pins down when it happened.

examples.greek: καὶ *τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ* γάμος ἐγένετο
examples.english: *On the third day*, a wedding took place
examples.note: A point on the calendar.

cards.name: Means
cards.eli5: The thing you used. “Cutting himself with stones.” The stones did not choose to.

formula.note: A thing, not a person.

cards.oneLine: The impersonal thing the action was done with.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — M: means, the tool.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A tool has no will of its own. If the dative could have refused, it is agency, not means.
cards.spotIt: Ask: with what? And check the answer is a thing.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the impersonal means by which the action of a given verb is accomplished.

examples.note: Stones are a tool. They did not decide anything.

cards.name: Agency
cards.eli5: The person who did it. “Led by the Spirit.”

formula.note: A person, not a thing.

cards.oneLine: The personal agent by whom the action was done.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — A: agency, the doer.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Same “by”, but somebody chose it. Means is the hammer; agency is the carpenter.
cards.spotIt: Ask: by whom? And check the answer is a person.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the personal agency by which the action of a given verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Means and agency are the same shape on the page. The only test is whether the dative has a will.

examples.english: But if you are led *by the Spirit*
examples.note: The Spirit chooses. That makes it agency.

cards.name: Manner
cards.eli5: How you did it. “He spoke openly.”

formula.note: Turn it into an -ly word.

cards.oneLine: The style in which the action was done.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — M: manner, the how.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not what you used, but the style you did it in. If an -ly word is the natural English, this is it.
cards.spotIt: Ask: how? Check that an -ly adverb fits.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the manner in which the action of a given verb is accomplished.
cards.watchOut: Means answers “with what tool”. Manner answers “in what style”.

examples.note: Openly is a style, not a tool.

cards.name: Association
cards.eli5: Who came along. “Buried with him.” You went together.

formula.note: Alongside — not used as a tool.

cards.oneLine: The one the action is done alongside.
cards.mnemonic: MAMA — A: association, the company.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Also “with”, but company rather than tool. The verb often starts with συν-, which gives it away.
cards.spotIt: Ask: with whom, in the sense of together with? Look for a συν- verb.
cards.bookDef: Denotes the person or thing with which a person is associated or by which a person is accompanied.
cards.watchOut: Three uses come out as “with”: means (a tool), manner (a style), association (company).

examples.english: Having been buried *with him* in baptism
examples.note: συν- on the verb, and you were buried alongside him, not using him.

cards.name: Cause
cards.eli5: Why it happened. “I am dying of hunger.” Hunger is the reason.

formula.note: = because of X.

cards.oneLine: The reason or basis for the action.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — B: because.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Slot “because of” in front and the sense holds. The reason can be outside you or inside you.
cards.spotIt: Ask: why? Then try “because of”.
cards.bookDef: Indicates the basis or reason of the action of a given verb, whether external (occasion) or internal (motivation).

examples.note: Hunger is the reason, not the tool.

cards.name: Cognate Dative
cards.eli5: The word says the doing-word again. “They were astounded with a great astoundment.”

formula.note: Same stem, said twice.

cards.oneLine: A dative built from the same stem as its verb.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — E: echo, second case running.
cards.mnemonicWhy: You met the echo in the accusative. Greek doubles the word for force where English just says “utterly”.
cards.spotIt: Say the verb and the dative out loud. Same root, or same idea?
cards.bookDef: Use of a dative noun that is a cognate (of the same stem) to the verb it modifies either formally or conceptually.

examples.note: ἐξέστησαν and ἐκστάσει are the same stem. English flattens it to “utterly”.

cards.name: Apposition
cards.eli5: Two stickers, fourth time. “Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.” One person, two names.

formula.note: Same person, second name.

cards.oneLine: A second dative renaming the first.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — A: alias, fourth case running.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Nominative, accusative, genitive, dative — the name tag turns up in all four. Learn it once, keep it forever.
cards.spotIt: Two datives side by side, no verb between them, both pointing at the same thing.
cards.bookDef: Two related substantives refer to the same person or thing.

examples.english: by Beelzebul, *the ruler* of the demons
examples.note: ἄρχοντι renames Βεελζεβούλ.

cards.name: Direct Object
cards.eli5: Some doing-words want it dressed this way: trusting, obeying, serving, worshipping, thanking, following.

formula.note: The dative is the object.

cards.oneLine: The object of a verb that takes the dative instead of the accusative.
cards.mnemonic: BEAD — D: devoted verbs.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Look at the list — trusting, obeying, serving, worshipping, thanking, following. Every one is a verb of devotion. That is the whole category in one word.
cards.spotIt: A dative where you expected an accusative? Check whether the verb is one of devotion.
cards.bookDef: The dative occurs after certain verbs of trusting, obeying, serving, worshiping, thanksgiving, or following and functions as the direct object.
cards.watchOut: The genitive has a fussy-verb list too — feel it, want it, share it, rule it, leave it. The dative's list is devotion.

examples.note: εὐχαριστέω takes its object in the dative.

cards.name: Articular
cards.eli5: It has its “the”. ὁ λόγος — the word, with the little word in front.

formula.note: The article is present. That is all the word means.

cards.oneLine: A noun with the article on it.
cards.mnemonic: Articular — the joint is there.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ἄρθρον is Greek for a joint, and it is also the Greek word for the article. Arthritis is a complaint about joints. Articular means the joint is in place — the article is there.
cards.spotIt: ὁ, ἡ, τό or one of their forms sitting in front of the noun.
cards.watchOut: The chart uses this word rather than defining it — “the articular or non-articular vocative”, “the articular noun in the genitive”. It assumes you already know it.

examples.note: ὁ λόγος is articular — and in the same verse θεός is not, which is the whole argument.
Articular in Greek even though English drops the “the”.

cards.name: Anarthrous
cards.eli5: No “the” at all. λόγος standing on its own.

formula.note: The article is absent. That is all the word means — not what the absence implies.

cards.oneLine: A noun with no article on it.
cards.mnemonic: Anarthrous — ἀν- no, ἄρθρον joint. No joint, no article.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The same ἄρθρον, with the alpha privative bolted on the front — the same ἀν- that turns a theist into an atheist. No joint means no article.
cards.spotIt: A noun standing bare, with no ὁ, ἡ or τό in front of it.
cards.watchOut: Two things this word does not mean. It is not the chart's word — the chart says “the absence of the article”, so that is the phrasing an exam will use. And it never means “a”: what an absent article conveys is the three-way question under Poof.

examples.note: θεός is anarthrous. That is the fact; what it means is a separate question, and the answer is not “a god”.
Anarthrous and still perfectly definite — a proper name needs no article.

cards.name: Monadic Article
cards.eli5: There is only one of him. “The only Son” — there is no second one to confuse him with.
cards.oneLine: The article on something one-of-a-kind.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — M: Monadic, the only one there is.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not “the best of several” — there are no several. The sun, the devil, the only Son.
cards.spotIt: Ask whether a second one could even exist. If not, monadic.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.note: Monadic — there is only one of him.

cards.name: Abstract Article
cards.eli5: It points at the idea, not at one example of it. “Salvation” — the whole thing, not one rescue.
cards.oneLine: The article on an abstract noun, naming the concept.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — A: Abstract, the idea itself.
cards.mnemonicWhy: English usually drops the “the” here, which is why it is easy to miss: ἡ σωτηρία is just “salvation”.
cards.spotIt: An abstract noun with an article that English would not translate.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.note: Abstract — the idea itself, not one instance of it.

cards.name: Generic Article
cards.eli5: It points at all of them at once. “Beware of false prophets” — the whole breed, not particular men.
cards.oneLine: The article on a class as a class, rather than on one member of it.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — G: Generic, all of them at once.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The one letter of MAGPIE that is not particularising. The chart's sentence has two halves — “particularizes … or uses it generically” — and this is the second half.
cards.spotIt: Swap in “that kind of thing” and see if it still works. If it does, generic.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: This is the odd one out. The other five particularise; this one generalises.

examples.english: Be on your guard against *false prophets*
examples.note: Generic — the whole class of them, not particular ones.

cards.name: Par Excellence
cards.eli5: Not a prophet — THE Prophet. The one who deserves the name more than anyone.
cards.oneLine: The article marking the one that best deserves the title.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — P: Par excellence, the one worth the name.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Say it out loud with the stress on “the”. If “THE Prophet” sounds right, that is this one.
cards.spotIt: Try putting the stress on “the”. THE Christ, THE Prophet, THE day.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: Close to monadic. Monadic means there is only one; par excellence means there are several and this is the one that counts.

examples.note: Par excellence — not a prophet, THE prophet.

cards.name: Simple Identification
cards.eli5: It just picks out which one you mean. The plain job, and the commonest.
cards.oneLine: The article singling out one particular person or thing.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — I: Identification, this one here.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The default. If none of the other five fit, it is doing the plain job of saying which one.
cards.spotIt: Nothing clever going on — it just tells you which one is meant.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.

examples.greek: ποῦ ἐστιν *ὁ* τεχθεὶς βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων
examples.english: Where is *he* who has been born King of the Jews?
examples.note: Identification — it picks out one particular person.

cards.name: Anaphoric Article
cards.eli5: It means “that one, the one I just said”. The water he was talking about a moment ago.
cards.oneLine: The article pointing back at something already named.
cards.mnemonic: MAGPIE — E: Earlier, the one already mentioned.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Translate it “that” instead of “the” and see if the sentence improves. If it does, it is anaphoric — and E is for Earlier, because the thing was named earlier.
cards.spotIt: Look backwards. Was this noun introduced a sentence or two ago without an article? Then this article is pointing at it.
cards.bookDef: The article particularizes a substantive or uses it generically.
cards.watchOut: The most common of the five in narrative, and the easiest to read straight past.

examples.greek: πόθεν οὖν ἔχεις *τὸ* ὕδωρ τὸ ζῶν
examples.english: So where do You get *that* ‘living water’?
examples.note: Anaphoric — the water already mentioned. Translate it “that”.

cards.name: Article as Personal Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article is the subject all by itself. “And they said to him.”
cards.oneLine: ὁ / οἱ standing alone as he, she or they — usually with δέ.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Personal: ὁ δέ means “and he”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ὁ δέ and οἱ δέ are so common in narrative they are worth learning as a phrase: “and he …”, “and they …”.
cards.spotIt: An article with no noun, carrying δέ, at the head of a clause.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.note: Personal — the article is the subject on its own.

cards.name: Article as Relative Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article starts a “who” clause. “Your Father who is in heaven.”
cards.oneLine: The article introducing a phrase that describes the noun before it.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Relative: the article that means “who”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: It is a chain link: the article hooks the phrase behind it onto the noun in front of it.
cards.spotIt: An article repeated after a noun, with a phrase rather than a noun after it.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.greek: τὸν πατέρα ὑμῶν *τὸν* ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
examples.note: Relative — the article introduces the clause.

cards.name: Article as Possessive Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article means “his”. Greek does not bother with αὐτοῦ when it is obvious.
cards.oneLine: The article doing the work of a possessive pronoun.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Possessive: the article that means “his”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: If the owner is obvious from the sentence, Greek leaves the possessive out and lets the article carry it. English has to put it back.
cards.spotIt: An article where English needs “his”, “her” or “their” and there is no genitive pronoun to supply it.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.english: And he divided *his* property between them
examples.note: Possessive — no αὐτοῦ needed, the article carries it.

cards.name: Article as Demonstrative Pronoun
cards.eli5: The article means “those”. “Those in the boat worshipped him.”
cards.oneLine: The article standing in for this, that, these or those.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Demonstrative: the article that means “those”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Usually with a phrase hanging off it: οἱ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ — “those in the boat”.
cards.spotIt: An article with no noun, followed by a prepositional phrase.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.note: Demonstrative — “those”.

cards.name: Article as Alternate Pronoun
cards.eli5: Two articles taking turns. “Some as apostles… others as prophets.”
cards.oneLine: ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ, dividing a group into some and others.
cards.mnemonic: Pronoun — Alternate: μέν … δέ, some … others.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The tell is the pair of little words. μέν sets up “on the one hand”, δέ answers “on the other”.
cards.spotIt: μέν on one article and δέ on another, splitting a list in two.
cards.bookDef: The article functions as a personal, relative, possessive, demonstrative, or alternate pronoun.

examples.note: Alternate — μέν … δέ, some … others.

cards.name: Absence — Indefinite
cards.eli5: No “the”, and it really does mean “a”. A boat. Any boat.
cards.oneLine: The missing article marking something non-particular: one of many.
cards.mnemonic: Poof — Indefinite: it really is “a”.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is the reading everyone reaches for first, and it is right about a third of the time. Ask the other two before settling.
cards.spotIt: Would “a” or “some” read naturally? Then indefinite.
cards.bookDef: The absence of the article may convey that a given substantive is non-particular (indefinite or qualitative) or definite. If definite, this may be in conjunction with a proper name, a prepositional object, ordinal numbers, in predicate nominatives, as the complement in an object, complement construction, with monadic (one-of-a-kind) nouns, with abstract or generic nouns, with a pronominal adjective, or with technical expressions.

examples.english: to have *a small boat* ready for him
examples.note: Indefinite — genuinely “a”.

cards.name: Absence — Qualitative
cards.eli5: No “the”, and it is pointing at the quality itself. “Full of grace” — grace-ness, not a portion of grace.
cards.oneLine: The missing article stressing the nature of the thing rather than its identity.
cards.mnemonic: Poof — Qualitative: the stuff itself, not a piece of it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Also non-particular, like indefinite — but the emphasis is on what kind, not on which one. Add “the very nature of” in your head and see if it fits.
cards.spotIt: Would “the quality of” or “the very nature of” fit in front of it? Then qualitative.
cards.bookDef: The absence of the article may convey that a given substantive is non-particular (indefinite or qualitative) or definite. If definite, this may be in conjunction with a proper name, a prepositional object, ordinal numbers, in predicate nominatives, as the complement in an object, complement construction, with monadic (one-of-a-kind) nouns, with abstract or generic nouns, with a pronominal adjective, or with technical expressions.

examples.note: Qualitative — the qualities themselves.

cards.name: Absence — Definite Anyway
cards.eli5: No “the”, and it still means THE. Paul does not need an article to be Paul.
cards.oneLine: The missing article where the noun is definite regardless — and the chart lists nine places it happens.
cards.mnemonic: Poof — Definite: gone, and still THE.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is the reading that settles John 1:1. Anarthrous does not mean indefinite; there are nine standard places where the article is simply not needed.
cards.spotIt: Run the list: is it a name, after a preposition, an ordinal, a predicate nominative, a complement, one-of-a-kind, abstract or generic, a pronominal adjective, or a technical term? Any of those and it is definite.
cards.bookDef: The absence of the article may convey that a given substantive is non-particular (indefinite or qualitative) or definite. If definite, this may be in conjunction with a proper name, a prepositional object, ordinal numbers, in predicate nominatives, as the complement in an object, complement construction, with monadic (one-of-a-kind) nouns, with abstract or generic nouns, with a pronominal adjective, or with technical expressions.
cards.watchOut: This is the row that settles John 1:1. Anarthrous does not mean indefinite.

examples.note: Definite — a proper name needs no article.
Definite — object of a preposition.
Definite — a predicate nominative with no article, and still THE Son.

cards.name: Granville Sharp Rule
cards.eli5: One “the” over two names joined by “and” — usually one person, not two.

formula.note: One article ⇒ one person.

cards.oneLine: One article governing two joined substantives points at a single person.
cards.mnemonic: Sharp joins.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The conditions are the rule: singular, personal, not proper names, same case, joined by καί. Miss one condition and it does not apply.
cards.spotIt: One article, then καί, then two singular personal non-proper nouns in the same case.
cards.bookDef: When a single article governs two singular, personal, non-proper substantives of the same case that are joined by καί, they frequently refer to the same person.
cards.watchOut: Proper names are excluded, and so are plurals. The rule is narrow on purpose.

examples.greek: *τοῦ* μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
examples.english: our great *God and Savior*, Jesus Christ
examples.note: One article covers both, so God and Savior are one person.

cards.name: Colwell's Rule
cards.eli5: Put a “the” word in front of “is” and it drops its “the”. That is why John 1:1 has no “the” on God.

formula.note: Definite, and the article is gone anyway.

cards.oneLine: A definite predicate nominative before the copula usually goes without the article.
cards.mnemonic: Colwell drops.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is why John 1:1 reads θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος with nothing in front of θεός — and why “a god” does not follow from the missing article.
cards.spotIt: A predicate nominative, no article, sitting in front of the to-be verb.
cards.bookDef: A definite predicate nominative does not usually take the article when preceding the copula (linking verb).
cards.watchOut: Read the rule in the direction it is written. It says definite nouns usually drop the article. It does not say every article-less noun before a copula is definite.

examples.note: θεός is definite and drops the article because it comes first.

cards.name: Apollonius's Canon
cards.eli5: “The Word of the God”, or “Word of God”. Never one of each.

formula.note: λόγος θεοῦ works too. One of each does not.

cards.oneLine: In a genitive chain, head noun and genitive both take the article or both go without.
cards.mnemonic: Apollonius matches.
cards.mnemonicWhy: They dress alike. ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, or λόγος θεοῦ — you do not get one of each.
cards.spotIt: A noun with a genitive after it. Check whether both carry the article, or neither.
cards.bookDef: When two nouns are in a genitive construction, both the head noun and the noun in the genitive case either have or lack the article.

examples.note: Both have the article.
Neither has it. Still the same construction.

cards.name: Agreement — Case, Number, Gender
cards.eli5: The describing word has to dress like the word it describes. Same case, same number, same gender — all three.

formula.note: Two out of three is not a match.

cards.oneLine: An adjective agrees with its noun in case, number and gender.
cards.mnemonic: Three reels, and all three have to line up.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A fruit machine pays out only when every reel matches. An adjective describes a noun only when case, number and gender all agree — and that is what tells you which noun it belongs to when Greek word order scatters them across the clause.
cards.spotIt: Found an adjective? Check case, number and gender against the noun before you decide what it modifies. Then look at where the article sits, which is what separates attributive from predicate.
cards.watchOut: Agreement is not in the summary chart — it is assumed there. Every row describes what an adjective does once it already agrees. And the substantival adjective is the exception that proves it: with no noun to agree with, its own gender and number tell you who is meant — οἱ ἅγιοι, masculine plural, is “the holy ones”.

examples.note: Two adjectives, each matching its own noun and not the other: δένδρον ἀγαθόν is neuter singular, καρποὺς καλούς masculine plural accusative. The endings are what keep them apart.
Masculine singular nominative all the way through, article included. Agreement plus the repeated article is what makes it attributive rather than a claim.

cards.name: The Article's Position
cards.eli5: Where the little word “the” sits tells you which kind it is. In front of the describing word, it describes. Only in front of the thing, it is a claim. In front of neither, you cannot tell.

formula.note: Same three words, four orders, three different answers.

cards.oneLine: Where the article sits decides attributive or predicate — unless there is no article at all.
cards.mnemonic: Follow the article. If it reaches the adjective, the adjective sticks.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The article is a hand. If it reaches past the noun and takes the adjective too, they come out as one phrase. If it only ever holds the noun, the adjective is left outside with nothing to do but assert. If it is holding nothing, nobody can tell you which was meant.
cards.spotIt: Find the article. Immediately before the adjective — directly, or by being repeated? Attributive. Before the noun and never before the adjective? Predicate. On neither word? Genuinely either, and only context decides.
cards.watchOut: The one case the test cannot settle is no article on either word. ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός is “a good man” or “a man is good” — the form will not tell you, and only the context will.

examples.note: Article straight into the adjective. Attributive, and it labels.
Adjective out in front, article on the noun. Predicate, and there is no verb written at all.

cards.name: Attributive
cards.eli5: It describes the noun. “The TRUE God.”

formula.note: The adjective sticks to the noun.

cards.oneLine: The adjective giving the noun a quality.
cards.mnemonic: ASAP — A: attributive, it sticks to the noun.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The article reaches past the noun and takes hold of the adjective, which is why they come out as one phrase: the true God. Say adjective and noun together and nothing is being claimed — it is a label.
cards.spotIt: Look at where the article is. Attributive when the article precedes the adjective — ὁ ἀγαθὸς λόγος, or ὁ λόγος ὁ ἀγαθός. Then confirm it reads as “the ___ noun”.
cards.bookDef: An adjective that ascribes a particular quality to a noun or substantive.
cards.watchOut: The position test needs an article to read. With none on either word — πολλῶν στρουθίων, Matt 10:31 — the form is genuinely ambiguous and context is what settles it, not a quick look at whether it labels or claims.

examples.note: With the article. One phrase, one idea.

examples.english: you are worth more than *many* sparrows
examples.note: Without the article, and still attributive.

cards.name: Substantival
cards.eli5: The adjective becomes the noun. “The Holy One” — no noun needed.

formula.note: The noun is missing and nobody minds.

cards.oneLine: The adjective acting as a noun.
cards.mnemonic: ASAP — S: substantival, it becomes the noun.
cards.mnemonicWhy: It usually takes the article, and that is the giveaway: ὁ ἅγιος, the Holy One.
cards.spotIt: An adjective with an article and no noun anywhere for it to describe.
cards.bookDef: The adjective normally takes on the characteristics of a noun (e.g., the article) and functions as a noun or substantive in a given phrase.

examples.note: No noun after it. The adjective is the noun.

cards.name: Adverbial
cards.eli5: The adjective jumps to the doing-word. “Going a little farther.”

formula.note: It modifies the verb, not a noun.

cards.oneLine: The adjective modifying a verb.
cards.mnemonic: ASAP — A: adverbial, it jumps to the verb.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Usually neuter accusative singular — and you have met this exact word before, as the accusative of measure. Same μικρόν, same verse.
cards.spotIt: An adjective answering how or how far, describing no noun at all.
cards.bookDef: Use of an adjective (usually in the neuter accusative singular) to modify a verb rather than noun.

examples.greek: καὶ προελθὼν *μικρὸν* ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ
examples.english: Going *a little farther*, he fell facedown
examples.note: The same word the accusative chapter files under measure. Two chapters, one form.

cards.name: Predicate
cards.eli5: It says something about the subject. “God is faithful.”

formula.note: A claim, not a label.

cards.oneLine: The adjective asserting a quality of the subject.
cards.mnemonic: ASAP — P: predicate, it makes a claim.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The article stays on the noun and never reaches the adjective, which leaves the adjective outside the phrase with nothing to do but assert: πιστὸς ὁ θεός is “God is faithful” with the verb left out.
cards.spotIt: Look at where the article is. Predicate when the article precedes the noun and not the adjective — ἀγαθὸς ὁ λόγος, or ὁ λόγος ἀγαθός. Supply “is” and it reads as a claim.
cards.bookDef: An adjective that predicates a certain quality to the subject, frequently by way of a copulative (linking) verb.
cards.watchOut: Attributive and predicate is the pair that gets missed, and the article's position settles it whenever there is one. With none on either word — μακάριος ἀνήρ, Rom 4:8 — it could be either as far as the form goes, and only context decides.

examples.note: No verb written. The adjective still makes the claim.

examples.greek: *μακάριος* ἀνὴρ οὗ οὐ μὴ λογίσηται κύριος ἁμαρτίαν
examples.english: *blessed* is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin
examples.note: Without the article, and still a claim.

cards.name: Superlative
cards.eli5: Best of three or more. “Most High God.”

ladder: Or add -τατος: ἅγιος holy → ἁγιώτατος, holiest.

cards.oneLine: Comparing three or more.
cards.mnemonic: SPECS — S: superlative, the -est.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Two endings, both meaning -est. -ιστος even looks like it if you squint: μέγιστος, great-est. -τατος is the other one, and it is the comparative's -τερος with the vowels swapped — τερος for two, τατος for the top.
cards.spotIt: Ask how many are being compared. Three or more ⇒ superlative.
cards.bookDef: Compares the qualities of three or more entities.
cards.watchOut: Two of the -ιστος words are not built off the adjective beside them: πλεῖστος does not come from πολύς's stem and ἐλάχιστος does not come from μικρός's. Those pairs are learned whole, like good and best. And a superlative form with nothing to compare it against is elative — it just means “very”.

examples.english: Jesus, Son of the *Most High* God
examples.note: Highest of all, not higher than one other.

examples.english: it is the *smallest* of all the seeds
examples.note: A comparative form doing superlative work — “smaller than all” is how Greek often says “smallest”.

cards.name: Positive
cards.eli5: Nothing is being compared. “The law is spiritual” — just what sort of thing it is.

formula.note: Kind, not degree.

cards.oneLine: The plain form, describing kind rather than degree.
cards.mnemonic: SPECS — P: positive, the plain one.
cards.mnemonicWhy: No -er, no -est, nothing to measure against. It just says what sort of thing it is.
cards.spotIt: No comparison anywhere in sight? Positive.
cards.bookDef: Focuses on the properties of a noun in terms of kind rather than degree.
cards.watchOut: This is the form the other two are built from: add -τερος for the comparative, -ιστος or -τατος for the superlative. A few words have no positive to build from — ὕψιστος, “most high”, never appears as a positive in the New Testament.

examples.note: Not more spiritual than anything. Just spiritual.

cards.name: Elative
cards.eli5: Not comparing at all — just turning it up. “A very large crowd.”

formula.note: No comparison. Just louder.

cards.oneLine: A comparative or superlative used to intensify, not to compare.
cards.mnemonic: SPECS — E: elative, the volume knob.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A -er or -est form with nothing to compare it against. Translate it “very”.
cards.spotIt: See a comparative or superlative, then look for what it is compared to. Nothing there? Elative.
cards.bookDef: Use of the comparative or superlative adjective to describe an intensification of the positive notion.

examples.note: Comparative form, elative sense — not more diligent than someone.
Superlative form, elative sense.

cards.name: Comparative
cards.eli5: More than one other. “More powerful than I am.”

ladder: Or, for the handful that have no such form, learn the word: μείζων, greater.

cards.oneLine: Comparing two, by degree.
cards.mnemonic: SPECS — C: comparative, the -er.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Greek builds it the way English does. Regular: bolt an ending on — μικρός small becomes μικρότερος smaller, and -τερος is doing the job of -er, which is also roughly what it sounds like. Irregular: a different word you simply learn, exactly like good → better and bad → worse.
cards.spotIt: Ask what it is being compared to. If there is an answer, comparative. If not, look at elative.
cards.bookDef: Focuses on the properties of a noun in terms of degree rather than kind.
cards.watchOut: πρεσβύτερος is literally “older”, and it is where presbyter and elder come from — the office is named with a comparative. And a comparative form does not always compare: with nothing on the other side of the scale it is elative, and means “very”.

examples.english: One who is *more powerful* than I am is coming after me
examples.note: μου is what he is more powerful than.

cards.name: Special Cases
cards.eli5: The words swap jobs. “More” can mean “most”: 1 Cor 13:13 says “greater” and means “greatest”.

formula.note: Everyday speech blurred the three.

cards.oneLine: One degree standing in for another.
cards.mnemonic: SPECS — S: special cases, the swaps.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Three swaps to know: positive for comparative, positive for superlative, and comparative for superlative. 1 Cor 13:13 literally says “more” and means “most”.
cards.spotIt: The form and the sense disagree. Translate by sense and name the swap.
cards.bookDef: Instances where popular speech and/or Semitic influence affected the use of the positive, comparative and superlative for one another.

examples.note: Positive form, comparative sense.
Positive form, superlative sense.

examples.english: but the *greatest* of these is love
examples.note: Comparative form, superlative sense. Three are in view, so “greater” means “greatest”.

cards.name: First Person Singular
cards.eli5: The one talking. Me.
cards.oneLine: ἐγώ — “I”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — I: ἐγώ.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ἐγώ is “ego”. Your ego is all about you — I.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: ἐγώ.
cards.bookDef: ἐγώ (“I”)

examples.note: ἐγώ εἰμι — “I am”. The verb ending already says “I”; the pronoun adds weight.

cards.name: Second Person Singular
cards.eli5: The one you are looking at. Just the one.
cards.oneLine: σύ — “you (one person)”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — You: σύ.
cards.mnemonicWhy: σύ is one finger, pointed at one face. One person, not a room.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: σύ.
cards.bookDef: σύ (“you” sg)

examples.note: Σὺ τίς εἶ; — “Who are YOU?” John 1:19. The pronoun is there to press.

cards.name: Third Person Singular
cards.eli5: Somebody else, one of them. He, she or it.
cards.oneLine: αὐτός, –ή, –ό — “he, she, it”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — He: αὐτός, –ή, –ό.
cards.mnemonicWhy: αὐτός sounds like AUTO — and an auto drives itSELF. That second meaning, “himself”, is the one you meet everywhere.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: αὐτός, –ή, –ό.
cards.bookDef: αὐτός, –ή, –ό (“he,” “she,” “it”)

examples.note: Three endings for three genders: –ός he, –ή she, –ό it.

cards.name: First Person Plural
cards.eli5: My lot. Me and the people with me.
cards.oneLine: ἡμεῖς — “we”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — We: ἡμεῖς.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ἡμεῖς has the H. H for Home team — us.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: ἡμεῖς.
cards.bookDef: ἡμεῖς (“we”)
cards.watchOut: ἡμεῖς and ὑμεῖς differ by one letter and mean opposite sides. ὑ = the u of YOU; ἡ = us.

examples.note: One letter from ὑμεῖς, and the two mean opposite sides.

cards.name: Second Person Plural
cards.eli5: Your lot. The whole room you are talking to.
cards.oneLine: ὑμεῖς — “you (more than one)”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — You all: ὑμεῖς.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ὑμεῖς starts with ὑ — the u of YOU.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: ὑμεῖς.
cards.bookDef: ὑμεῖς (“you” pl)
cards.watchOut: ἡμεῖς and ὑμεῖς differ by one letter and mean opposite sides. ὑ = the u of YOU; ἡ = us.

examples.note: English hides this and Greek does not. Most New Testament “you” is this one — plural, the church, not you personally.

cards.name: Third Person Plural
cards.eli5: Their lot. The other crowd.
cards.oneLine: αὐτοί, –αί, –ά — “they”.
cards.mnemonic: Roll call — They: αὐτοί, –αί, –ά.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The autos, plural. αὐτός becomes αὐτοί.
cards.spotIt: A nominative pronoun standing on its own: αὐτοί, –αί, –ά.
cards.bookDef: αὐτοί, –αί, –ά (they)

examples.note: Same three genders again: –οί, –αί, –ά.

cards.name: Simple Active
cards.eli5: He does it. Full stop. “God loved the world.”
cards.oneLine: The subject performs the action himself.
cards.mnemonic: Active — Do: he does it, and that is all.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The plain one, and the one you meet most. If nothing bends back and nothing is being allowed, it is simple.
cards.spotIt: Ask: is the subject doing it, and does none of it come back on him? Simple active.
cards.bookDef: The subject directly performs the action of the verb.

examples.note: God does the loving; it lands on the world, not on God.

cards.name: Causative Active
cards.eli5: He does not do it himself — he makes it happen. God makes the sun come up.
cards.oneLine: The subject is the reason it happens, not the one doing it.
cards.mnemonic: Active — Make: he makes it happen.
cards.mnemonicWhy: God does not personally shove the sun over the hill. He causes it to rise. Slip “causes … to” into your translation and see if it fits better.
cards.spotIt: Try “causes X to …” in English. If that reads better than the plain active, it is causative.
cards.bookDef: The subject is the cause behind the action of the verb.
cards.watchOut: The form is ordinary active. Nothing marks it — only the sense does.

examples.note: Active form, but the subject is the cause, not the doer.

cards.name: Reflexive Active
cards.eli5: He does it to himself — and says so with an extra word. “Train yourself.”

formula.note: Two words doing what the middle does in one.

cards.oneLine: An active verb plus a reflexive pronoun: σεαυτόν, ἑαυτόν.
cards.mnemonic: Active — Me: active verb, and a spare “self” lying next to it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is how the active does reflexive: it has to borrow a pronoun. The middle does not — that is the whole difference.
cards.spotIt: Active verb, and a reflexive pronoun (σεαυτόν, ἑαυτόν) sitting beside it.
cards.bookDef: The subject performs the action to himself.
cards.watchOut: Not the middle. The middle reflexive carries it in the verb and needs no pronoun.

examples.note: γύμναζε is active. σεαυτόν is doing the reflexive work.

cards.name: Reflexive Middle
cards.eli5: It comes straight back to him, and the verb says so on its own. Judas hanged himself.

formula.note: One word: he hanged himself.

cards.oneLine: A middle verb whose action lands on the subject — no reflexive pronoun needed.
cards.mnemonic: Middle — To me: the boomerang. It comes back.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The middle carries the “self” inside the ending. Where the active had to add σεαυτόν, the middle just is reflexive.
cards.spotIt: A middle-form verb, and the action clearly lands on the subject, with no reflexive pronoun in sight.
cards.bookDef: The subject performs the action to himself.
cards.watchOut: Compare 1 Tim 4:7: same idea, active verb, borrowed pronoun. The voice is the difference.

examples.note: One middle verb. The “himself” is in the ending.

cards.name: Middle of Special Interest
cards.eli5: He does it, and he is the one who gets the good of it. Mary picked the good bit for herself.
cards.oneLine: The subject does the action for his own benefit.
cards.mnemonic: Middle — For me: he did it, and he keeps the benefit.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not to himself — for himself. The action goes out; the profit comes back.
cards.spotIt: The subject acts, and the person who gains by it is the subject. Try “for himself” in the translation.
cards.bookDef: The subject performs the action for himself.
cards.watchOut: “To himself” is reflexive; “for himself” is special interest. One lands on him, one profits him.

examples.note: She chose, and she is the one who has it.

cards.name: Permissive Middle
cards.eli5: He does not do it and it is not forced on him — he lets it happen to him. “Get baptised.”
cards.gist: he lets it be done to him
cards.oneLine: The subject consents to the action happening to or for him.
cards.mnemonic: Middle — Let me: open hands. He allows it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: You do not baptise yourself and you are not ambushed either. You submit to it. That is the middle's permission.
cards.spotIt: Try “let himself be …” or “have it done”. If that is the sense, it is permissive.
cards.bookDef: The subject allows something to be done to or for himself.

examples.english: Get up, *be baptised*, and *wash away* your sins
examples.note: Both middle. Paul is told to let it be done to him.

cards.name: Simple Passive
cards.eli5: It happens to him. He did nothing. “The righteousness of God is revealed.”
cards.oneLine: The subject receives the action instead of doing it.
cards.mnemonic: Passive — Done to me: it arrives whether he moved or not.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The plain passive, and the easy one. The subject is the target, and somebody or something else did it.
cards.spotIt: The subject is not doing it. Ask “by whom?” and the answer is somewhere else, or nowhere.
cards.bookDef: The subject receives the action of the verb.

examples.note: It does not reveal itself. It is revealed.

cards.name: Permissive Passive
cards.eli5: It is done to him — but only because he says yes. “Be filled with the Spirit.”
cards.oneLine: A passive where the subject is being asked to consent, not just to receive.
cards.mnemonic: Passive — Let it be done: he opens the door.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A passive you can be commanded to do only makes sense if you have a say in it. That is the tell.
cards.spotIt: A passive form, but the sense is consent — often an imperative you are told to allow.
cards.bookDef: The subject gives consent or permission regarding the action of the verb.
cards.watchOut: Very close to the middle permissive. The middle is “he lets it be done to himself”; the passive is “he consents to what is done to him”.

examples.note: You do not fill yourself. You are told to let yourself be filled.

cards.name: Potential Indicative
cards.eli5: Somebody wants something. “I want them to marry.” The wanting is the fact.
cards.oneLine: A verb of wishing, wanting or obligation, with an infinitive hanging off it.
cards.mnemonic: WAIFS — W: Want.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The wanting really is happening, so the verb is indicative. What is wanted sits in the infinitive after it.
cards.spotIt: A verb like βούλομαι, θέλω or δεῖ, followed by an infinitive.
cards.bookDef: Used with verbs of obligation, wish, or desire, followed by a complementary infinitive.

examples.english: So I *want* younger women to marry
examples.note: βούλομαι is the indicative; γαμεῖν is the infinitive it wants.

cards.name: Interrogative
cards.eli5: It asks something — and the answer will be a plain fact too. “Who are you?”
cards.oneLine: A question expecting an answer in the indicative.
cards.mnemonic: WAIFS — A: Ask.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A question about what is actually the case. Not “should we?” — that is a different mood — but “who are you?”
cards.spotIt: A question mark, and the answer would be a statement of fact.
cards.bookDef: A question that will also be answered in the indicative mood.

examples.note: The answer comes back in the indicative too: “I am not the Christ.”

cards.name: Conditional Indicative
cards.eli5: “If this is true — and let us say it is.” The if-half is treated as a fact.

ladder: First class — εἰ + indicative: if this is so, and it is.
Second class — εἰ + indicative, ἄν in the apodosis: if this were so, but it is not.

cards.oneLine: The “if” half of a first or second class conditional, after εἰ.
cards.mnemonic: WAIFS — I: If.
cards.mnemonicWhy: εἰ takes you to the indicative. First class assumes the if is true; second class assumes it is false. Either way the speaker is treating it as settled.
cards.spotIt: εἰ plus an indicative verb. First class: assumed true. Second class: contrary to fact, and ἄν usually shows up in the second half.
cards.bookDef: First Class: The protasis (“if” clause) of a first class conditional sentence. · Second Class: The protasis of a second class conditional sentence.
cards.watchOut: εἰ + indicative is first or second class. ἐάν + subjunctive is third class, and that is a different card in a different mood.

examples.greek: εἰ οὖν *συνηγέρθητε* τῷ Χριστῷ, τὰ ἄνω ζητεῖτε
examples.english: So if you *have been raised* with Christ, seek the things above
examples.note: Assumed true: you have been raised. So — seek.

examples.greek: εἰ γὰρ *ἐπιστεύετε* Μωϋσεῖ, ἐπιστεύετε ἂν ἐμοί
examples.english: For if you *believed* Moses, you would believe me
examples.note: Contrary to fact: they do not believe Moses. Note the ἄν in the second half.

cards.name: Declarative
cards.eli5: It just says what is. “In the beginning was the Word.”
cards.oneLine: A plain statement, with nothing hedged.
cards.mnemonic: WAIFS — F: Fact.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The default, and the reason the indicative exists. If nothing else is going on, this is it.
cards.spotIt: A statement with no “if”, no question mark, and no wanting.
cards.bookDef: An unqualified assertion or statement.

examples.note: No hedge, no condition. It simply was.

cards.name: Cohortative
cards.eli5: A future that is really an order. “You shall love your neighbour.”
cards.oneLine: A future indicative doing the work of a command.
cards.mnemonic: WAIFS — S: Shall.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is how the Ten Commandments sound: “you shall not”. It is grammatically a prediction and functionally an order.
cards.spotIt: A future indicative where the sense is “do this”, not “this will happen”.
cards.bookDef: A future indicative that is used as a command.
cards.watchOut: Not the imperative mood. The form is future indicative — only the use is a command.

examples.note: Future in form. An order in force.

cards.name: Purpose
cards.eli5: Why he did it. “He came SO THAT he could tell people about the light.”
cards.oneLine: ἵνα (or ὅπως) plus subjunctive, giving the aim.
cards.mnemonic: Subjunctive — Aim: the arrow, before it lands.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Purpose is about intention. It might not even come off; it is what was aimed at.
cards.spotIt: ἵνα or ὅπως, and the sense is “in order to”.
cards.bookDef: Follows the particle ἵνα (or ὅπως) and expresses purpose (intended result).
cards.watchOut: Same word, ἵνα, as result. Only the sense separates them: aimed at, or actually happened.

examples.english: in order to *testify* about the light
examples.note: That is what he came for. The aim.

cards.name: Result
cards.eli5: What actually came of it. “…that he was born blind.” Nobody aimed at that.
cards.oneLine: ἵνα (or ὅπως) plus subjunctive, giving what actually followed.
cards.mnemonic: Subjunctive — Outcome: the bang, after it lands.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Same word as purpose. The test is whether anyone intended it. Nobody intends a baby to be born blind, so ἵνα there is result.
cards.spotIt: ἵνα, and “with the result that” reads better than “in order that”.
cards.bookDef: Follows the particle ἵνα (or ὅπως) and expresses result (actual result).

examples.english: Who sinned … that *he was born* blind?
examples.note: The blindness is the outcome, not anybody's aim.

cards.name: Conditional Subjunctive
cards.eli5: A real maybe. “If anyone keeps my word” — some will, some will not.
cards.oneLine: The “if” half of a third class conditional, after ἐάν.
cards.mnemonic: Subjunctive — If: the dice. Genuinely open.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ἐάν is εἰ + ἄν, and the ἄν is the uncertainty. εἰ alone goes with the indicative; ἐάν goes with the subjunctive.
cards.spotIt: ἐάν or ἐὰν μή, plus a subjunctive verb.
cards.bookDef: Follows the particle ἐάν or ἐὰν μή and is used in the protasis of a third class conditional sentence.
cards.watchOut: εἰ + indicative is first or second class. ἐάν + subjunctive is third. The particle tells you before the verb does.

examples.note: Third class. Open — some will, some will not.

cards.name: Indefinite Relative
cards.eli5: Not one named person — anybody at all. “Whoever calls on the name of the Lord.”
cards.oneLine: After an indefinite relative pronoun with ἄν, the verb goes subjunctive.
cards.mnemonic: Subjunctive — Whoever: a ticket with no name on it.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The ἄν is what makes it indefinite. ὅς is “who”; ὃς ἄν is “whoever it turns out to be”.
cards.spotIt: ὅστις (ἄν/ἐάν) or ὃς (δ᾿) ἄν, then a subjunctive.
cards.bookDef: Used after the indefinite relative pronouns ὅστις (ἄν/ἐάν) or ὃς (δ᾿) ἄν.

examples.greek: ὃς ἂν *ἐπικαλέσηται* τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται
examples.english: *whoever* calls on the name of the Lord will be saved
examples.note: No particular person is meant. Anyone who does it.

cards.name: Indefinite Temporal
cards.eli5: Not one particular time — any time it happens. “Whenever someone says…”
cards.oneLine: After ὅταν or another temporal word, the verb goes subjunctive.
cards.mnemonic: Subjunctive — Whenever: the alarm that could go off any time.
cards.mnemonicWhy: ὅταν is ὅτε + ἄν — “when” plus the same ἄν that made “whoever” indefinite. Same trick, applied to time.
cards.spotIt: ὅταν, or an “until” word: ἕως, ἄχρι, μέχρι. Then a subjunctive.
cards.bookDef: Used after the temporal conjunction ὅταν or after a temporal adverb or preposition (e.g., ἕως, ἄχρι, μέχρι).
cards.watchOut: ὅταν is the common one, but ἕως, ἄχρι and μέχρι — “until” words — pull the subjunctive too.

examples.note: Not one occasion. Every time it happens.

cards.name: Hortatory Subjunctive
cards.eli5: “Let us do good.” He is telling you to do it, and putting himself in with you.
cards.oneLine: A first person plural subjunctive: the speaker orders the room and joins it.
cards.mnemonic: On its own — Let us: he gives the order and stands in the queue with you.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is why it is not an imperative. An imperative points at you; the hortatory says “us”, and the speaker is inside the command.
cards.spotIt: A first person plural subjunctive, translated “let us …”.
cards.bookDef: The author commands his audience but also includes himself in the command.
cards.watchOut: Not the imperative. The imperative commands you; the hortatory commands us.

examples.note: Paul is not exempt from it. That is the whole point of the form.

cards.name: Deliberative Subjunctive
cards.eli5: “Should we keep sinning?” It asks — sometimes for an answer, sometimes to make a point.
cards.oneLine: A subjunctive asking a question, real or rhetorical.
cards.mnemonic: On its own — Should we: the raised eyebrow.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The indicative asks what is the case; the subjunctive asks what we should do about it. Rom 6:1 is not looking for information.
cards.spotIt: A question, and the verb is subjunctive rather than indicative.
cards.bookDef: Asks a real or rhetorical question.
cards.watchOut: The interrogative indicative asks about facts (“who are you?”). This one asks about what should be done.

examples.greek: *ἐπιμένωμεν* τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ
examples.english: *Should we continue* in sin so that grace may multiply?
examples.note: Rhetorical. The answer is coming in the next verse, and it is no.

cards.name: Emphatic Negation
cards.eli5: Two “no” words at once. Not just no — never, not a chance.
cards.oneLine: The double negative οὐ μή with a subjunctive: the strongest denial Greek has.
cards.mnemonic: On its own — Never: two negatives stacked, and they do not cancel.
cards.mnemonicWhy: In English two negatives make a positive. In Greek they make a shout. οὐ μή is the strongest no in the language.
cards.spotIt: The two words οὐ μή sitting together, then a subjunctive.
cards.bookDef: Expressed by the double negative οὐ μή, it strongly denies that something will happen.

examples.greek: *οὐ μὴ* *εἰσέλθητε* εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν
examples.english: you will *never* *enter* the kingdom of heaven
examples.note: Not “probably not”. Never.

cards.name: Prohibitory Subjunctive
cards.eli5: “Do not think that…” A “don't”, told with a subjunctive instead of a command.

ladder: aorist subjunctive — not present, not imperative.
Both, or it is not this.

cards.oneLine: A negated aorist subjunctive doing the work of “do not”.
cards.mnemonic: On its own — Don't: μή out front, aorist behind.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Two conditions, both required: the command is negated, and the subjunctive is aorist. Miss either and it is something else.
cards.spotIt: μή plus an aorist subjunctive. Both parts have to be there.
cards.bookDef: Used when two conditions are met: (1) the command is negated, and (2) the subjunctive uses the aorist tense-form.
cards.watchOut: Compare the imperative's prohibition (μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε, 1 John 2:15). Same idea, different mood — the tell is which form follows the μή.

examples.greek: *μὴ* *νομίσητε* ὅτι ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὸν νόμον ἢ τοὺς προφήτας
examples.english: *Do not think* that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets
examples.note: μή, and νομίσητε is aorist subjunctive. Both boxes ticked.

cards.name: Request
cards.eli5: It is shaped like an order but you are talking to somebody above you, so it lands as “please”.
cards.oneLine: An imperative aimed at a superior, which turns it into a request.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — P: Please.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Grammar cannot tell you this one. Who is being spoken to can. Nobody orders Jesus about; “help us” is a plea.
cards.spotIt: An imperative addressed to someone above the speaker.
cards.bookDef: A command that is given to a superior and is thus weakened to a request.

examples.english: If you can do anything … *help* us
examples.note: Imperative in form. Begging in force.

cards.name: Greeting
cards.eli5: “Greetings!” Nobody is being ordered to do anything. It is just how you say hello.
cards.oneLine: A set phrase that happens to be an imperative.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — H: Hi.
cards.mnemonicWhy: χαῖρε literally means “rejoice”, but nobody hears it that way — it is Greek for “hello”. A frozen form, like English “goodbye”.
cards.spotIt: χαῖρε or χαίρετε used to open a conversation.
cards.bookDef: Greetings are often expressed with a stereotyped imperative.

examples.note: Judas is not commanding Jesus to rejoice.

cards.name: Permission
cards.eli5: Not an order — a shrug. “If he wants to go, let him go.”
cards.oneLine: An imperative that allows something rather than demanding it.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — O: OK.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Paul is not commanding anybody to leave. He is saying: if that is what happens, let it.
cards.spotIt: Try “let him …” in the translation. If that is the sense, it is permission, not command.
cards.bookDef: Used to convey permission, allowance, or toleration.

examples.english: If the unbeliever leaves, *let him leave*
examples.note: Allowance, not instruction.

cards.name: Prohibition
cards.eli5: A command with a “not” in front. “Do not love the world.”
cards.oneLine: A negated imperative: it forbids.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — N: No.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Greek negates commands with μή, never οὐ. See μή in front of an imperative and it is a prohibition.
cards.spotIt: μή plus an imperative.
cards.bookDef: A negative command that forbids an action.
cards.watchOut: μή + present imperative is this. μή + aorist subjunctive is the prohibitory subjunctive. The form after μή decides.

examples.note: μή plus a present imperative.

cards.name: Conditional Imperative
cards.eli5: It looks like two orders, but the first is really an “if”. “Come and see” means “if you come, you will see”.
cards.gist: come and see = if you come
cards.oneLine: An imperative standing in for the “if” half of a condition.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — I: If.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Two imperatives joined by καί, where the first is the condition of the second. English does it too: “touch that and you're dead.”
cards.spotIt: Two imperatives with καί, and the sense is “if the first, then the second”.
cards.bookDef: Like the subjunctive, an imperative can be used to state a condition.

examples.english: *Come* and see — that is, if you come, you will see
examples.note: Philip is not barking two orders. He is offering a deal.

cards.name: Command
cards.eli5: Just do it. “Rejoice always!”
cards.oneLine: The plain imperative: an exhortation or a charge.
cards.mnemonic: PHONIC — C: Charge.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The default. If nobody is being softened, allowed, greeted or conditioned, it is a straight command.
cards.spotIt: An imperative with no μή, no καί-condition, and no superior being addressed.
cards.bookDef: An exhortation or charge.
cards.watchOut: Same word as the greeting card (χαίρω). Context decides whether it is “hello” or “rejoice”.

examples.note: The same verb as the greeting — here it means it.

cards.name: Voluntative Optative
cards.eli5: A wish said over somebody. “May grace and peace be multiplied to you.”
cards.oneLine: The optative of prayer, blessing and benediction.
cards.mnemonic: Optative — May: the candle you light over somebody.
cards.mnemonicWhy: This is where you actually meet the optative: the openings and closings of letters. If it reads like a benediction, it is this one.
cards.spotIt: Translate with “may …”. Prayers, blessings and the famous μὴ γένοιτο.
cards.bookDef: Expresses a prayer, benediction, blessing, or wish.

examples.english: *May* grace and peace *be multiplied* to you
examples.note: A blessing, not a prediction.

cards.name: Deliberative Optative
cards.eli5: Somebody wonders what something means. “They asked what this parable might be.”
cards.oneLine: The optative in an indirect or rhetorical question.
cards.mnemonic: Optative — Might: the question you ask sideways.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Not a direct question. It is reported: they asked what it might be. English does the same softening.
cards.spotIt: A reported question, usually after a verb of asking, with “might” fitting the translation.
cards.bookDef: Used with indirect (rhetorical) questions.
cards.watchOut: The deliberative subjunctive asks directly, “should we?”. This one is reported: “they asked what it might be.”

examples.greek: ἐπηρώτων δὲ αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ τίς αὕτη *εἴη* ἡ παραβολή
examples.english: His disciples questioned him as to what this parable *might be*
examples.note: The question is reported, not quoted. Hence the optative.

cards.name: Potential Optative
cards.eli5: The furthest-out maybe there is. “Even if you should suffer…” — unlikely, but suppose it.

ladder: First class — εἰ + indicative: and it is so.
Second class — εἰ + indicative + ἄν: but it is not.
Third class — ἐάν + subjunctive: it may well be.
Fourth class — εἰ + optative: it probably is not, but suppose.

cards.oneLine: The optative in a fourth class conditional.
cards.mnemonic: Optative — Should: the four-leaf clover. Fourth class, and about as common.
cards.mnemonicWhy: First class assumes true, second contrary to fact, third a real maybe, fourth a remote one — and the fourth needs the optative. The clover is your reminder that it is number four and it is rare.
cards.spotIt: εἰ plus an optative. Translate “if … should”.
cards.bookDef: Involves a fourth class conditional clause.
cards.watchOut: Now you have all four: εἰ + indicative (1st, 2nd), ἐάν + subjunctive (3rd), εἰ + optative (4th).

examples.english: Even if *you should suffer* for righteousness, you are blessed
examples.note: Remote. Peter is not saying it will happen.

cards.name: Present
cards.eli5: Happening now, and still rolling. “I am loosing.”
cards.oneLine: λύω — “I am loosing”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Am: λύω.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Am — the helper English reaches for when something is going on right now.
cards.spotIt: No augment, no sigma, no reduplication — the bare stem.
cards.bookDef: PRESENT · λύω · “I am loosing”

examples.note: The default. Every other form is this one with something added to it.

cards.name: Future
cards.eli5: Not yet. “I will loose.”
cards.oneLine: λύσω — “I will loose”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Will: λύσω.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Will — the helper for what has not happened yet. The σ is the promise.
cards.spotIt: A σ after the stem and no augment in front.
cards.bookDef: FUTURE · λύσω · “I will loose”

examples.note: The same σ as the aorist. The augment is what separates them: the aorist has one, the future does not.

cards.name: Imperfect
cards.eli5: Was going on, back then. “I was loosing.”
cards.oneLine: ἔλυον — “I was loosing”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Was: ἔλυον.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Was — the helper for something that kept going, back then.
cards.spotIt: An ἐ- augment on the front and no σ.
cards.bookDef: IMPERFECT · ἔλυον · “I was loosing”

examples.note: Past and still rolling. Compare the aorist, which is past and done with.

cards.name: Aorist
cards.eli5: It happened. One snapshot, no comment. “I loosed.”
cards.oneLine: ἔλυσα — “I loosed”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Did: ἔλυσα.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Did — no fuss and no duration. One snapshot of the whole thing.
cards.spotIt: Augment and σ together: ἔ-λυ-σα.
cards.bookDef: AORIST · ἔλυσα · “I loosed”

examples.note: The workhorse of narrative. It says that it happened, not how long it took.

cards.name: Perfect
cards.eli5: Done, and it still stands. “I have loosed.”
cards.oneLine: λέλυκα — “I have loosed”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Have: λέλυκα.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Have — finished, and you are still holding what it left behind.
cards.spotIt: The stem said twice at the front — λέ-λυκα.
cards.bookDef: PERFECT · λέλυκα · “I have loosed”

examples.note: Reduplication is the perfect's fingerprint. Once you see the doubled front you can stop looking.

cards.name: Pluperfect
cards.eli5: Done before the thing you are already talking about. “I had loosed.”
cards.oneLine: ἐλελύκειν — “I had loosed”.
cards.mnemonic: Clock tower — Had: ἐλελύκειν.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Had — finished before the thing you were already talking about.
cards.spotIt: Reduplication and an augment together: ἐ-λε-λύκειν.
cards.bookDef: PLUPERFECT · ἐλελύκειν · “I had loosed”
cards.watchOut: The chart is only the indicative. Outside the indicative there is no time — only aspect, which is what the chapter says is the dominant force anyway.

examples.note: The perfect pushed one step further back, and rare in the New Testament.

confusions.question: Predicate nominative or apposition?
confusions.test: Is there a verb?
confusions.answer: Verb ⇒ predicate nominative, a claim. Comma only ⇒ apposition, a label.
confusions.example: “Ivan is the student” (claim) vs “Ivan, the student, came to class” (label).

confusions.question: Absolute or hanging?
confusions.test: Does a pronoun later in the sentence pick the word back up?
confusions.answer: No rope ⇒ absolute. Hangs by a pronoun ⇒ hanging.
confusions.example: Mark 1:1 “The beginning of the gospel…” (a headline) vs Matt. 13:38 “the good seed — THESE are the sons…” (a rope).

confusions.question: Address or subject?
confusions.test: Talked about, or talked to?
confusions.answer: About ⇒ subject. To ⇒ address, however much it looks like a subject.
confusions.example: “Husbands love their wives” (subject) vs “Husbands, love your wives” (address).

confusions.question: Two nominatives, one verb — which is the subject?
confusions.test: Run PAP: pronoun, then article, then proper name.
confusions.answer: First yes wins. In John 1:1c ὁ λόγος has the article, so it is the subject and θεός is the predicate — definite, not “a god”.
confusions.example: καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.

confusions.question: Cognate or plain direct object?
confusions.test: Does the object echo the verb — same root, or same idea?
confusions.answer: Echo ⇒ cognate. No echo ⇒ just the object. Either way it is still the object.
confusions.example: “Fight the good fight” (echo) vs “I hit Ivan” (no echo).

confusions.question: Two accusatives side by side — renamed, or called something?
confusions.test: Is there a verb doing the naming?
confusions.answer: A verb calls, makes or gives it something ⇒ complement. No verb between them, the second just says which one exactly ⇒ apposition.
confusions.example: “I have called you FRIENDS” · “they chose Stephen, a man full of faith”.

confusions.question: Accusative of respect or direct object?
confusions.test: Put “with respect to” in front of it.
confusions.answer: Better ⇒ respect. Worse ⇒ direct object.
confusions.example: “pierced WITH RESPECT TO the heart” — better. “I hit WITH RESPECT TO Ivan” — worse.

confusions.question: Subjective or objective?
confusions.test: Turn the head noun into a verb. Is X doing it, or getting it?
confusions.answer: Doing it ⇒ subjective. Getting it ⇒ objective.
confusions.example: “the love of Christ” — Christ loving (subjective) or Christ being loved (objective). The Greek is identical either way.

confusions.question: Source or separation? Both say “from”.
confusions.test: Is the “from” attached to a noun or to a verb?
confusions.answer: Where a noun came from ⇒ source. What a verb moves away from ⇒ separation.
confusions.example: “the righteousness from God” (source) vs “depart from the faith” (separation).

confusions.question: Genitive direct object or objective genitive?
confusions.test: What is the genitive hanging off — a verb or a noun?
confusions.answer: Off a verb ⇒ genitive direct object. Off a noun ⇒ objective genitive.
confusions.example: “you did not lack anything” (verb) vs “faith in God” (noun).

confusions.question: Partitive or material/content?
confusions.test: Is the genitive the whole the head noun is a slice of, or the stuff the head noun is made of?
confusions.answer: Whole ⇒ partitive. Stuff ⇒ material or content.
confusions.example: “one of the boats” (a slice of the fleet) vs “a cup of water” (what fills the cup).

confusions.question: Possession or relationship?
confusions.test: Is the genitive owning a thing, or being kin to a person?
confusions.answer: Owns a thing ⇒ possession. Family, with “son of” or “wife of” left out ⇒ relationship.
confusions.example: “the house of Philip” (owns it) vs “James the [son] of Zebedee” (kin).

confusions.question: Attributive or description?
confusions.test: Can the genitive be rewritten as an adjective?
confusions.answer: Becomes a real adjective ⇒ attributive. Nothing more specific fits ⇒ description, the catch-all.
confusions.example: “the word of his power” → “his powerful word” (attributive) vs “a baptism of repentance” (description).

confusions.question: Vocative, or nominative of address?
confusions.test: What shape is the word in?
confusions.answer: Vocative shape ⇒ vocative of direct address. Nominative shape doing the same job ⇒ nominative of address.
confusions.example: Λάζαρε (vocative) vs οἱ ἄνδρες, “Husbands…” (nominative doing a vocative’s work).

confusions.question: Means or agency?
confusions.test: Could the dative have refused?
confusions.answer: A thing with no will ⇒ means. A person who chose ⇒ agency.
confusions.example: “cutting himself with stones” (means) vs “led by the Spirit” (agency).

confusions.question: Three uses all come out “with”. Which one?
confusions.test: Tool, style, or company?
confusions.answer: A tool ⇒ means. A style ⇒ manner. Company ⇒ association, often with a συν- verb.
confusions.example: “with stones” · “openly” · “buried with him”.

confusions.question: Place or sphere?
confusions.test: Could you point at it?
confusions.answer: A real spot ⇒ place. A realm you can only imagine ⇒ sphere.
confusions.example: “sitting in a circle” (place) vs “sighing in his spirit” (sphere).

confusions.question: Indirect object or personal interest?
confusions.test: Is the dative receiving a thing, or gaining and losing?
confusions.answer: Receives what was handed over ⇒ indirect object. Benefits or suffers ⇒ personal interest.
confusions.example: “give glory to God” (receives) vs “adorned for her husband” (benefits).

confusions.question: Attributive or predicate?
confusions.test: Where is the article? Does it precede the adjective, or only the noun?
confusions.answer: The article precedes the adjective ⇒ attributive: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός. The article precedes the noun and not the adjective ⇒ predicate: ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος. No article on either word ⇒ it could be either, and context decides: ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός.
confusions.example: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος “the good man” · ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος “the man is good” · ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός — either.

confusions.question: Comparative or elative?
confusions.test: Is there anything on the other side of the scale?
confusions.answer: Something to compare against ⇒ comparative. Nothing ⇒ elative, and translate it “very”.
confusions.example: “more powerful than I” (comparative) vs “a very large crowd” (elative).

confusions.question: No article — indefinite, or Colwell?
confusions.test: Is it a predicate nominative sitting in front of the to-be verb?
confusions.answer: In front of the copula ⇒ Colwell explains the missing article, and the noun can still be definite. Elsewhere, run the three questions: a? quality? or still THE?
confusions.example: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος — Colwell, definite. πλοιάριον in Mark 3:9 — genuinely “a”.

confusions.question: Two accusative objects — which double is it?
confusions.test: Slip “as” between them.
confusions.answer: “As” fits ⇒ object + complement. “As” is nonsense and one of them is a person ⇒ person + thing.
confusions.example: “gave his life AS a ransom” · “asks him for bread”.

confusions.question: He did it to himself — active or middle?
confusions.test: Is there a reflexive pronoun sitting next to the verb?
confusions.answer: A spare σεαυτόν / ἑαυτόν doing the work ⇒ active reflexive. The verb carries it alone, no pronoun ⇒ middle reflexive.
confusions.example: “γύμναζε σεαυτόν” (1 Tim 4:7, active) · “ἀπήγξατο” (Matt 27:5, middle).

confusions.question: ἵνα + subjunctive — purpose or result?
confusions.test: Did anybody aim at this?
confusions.answer: Somebody intended it ⇒ purpose, “in order that”. It just turned out that way ⇒ result, “with the result that”.
confusions.example: “came to testify” (John 1:7) · “that he was born blind” (John 9:2).

confusions.question: An “if” clause — which class?
confusions.test: Look at the particle before you look at the verb.
confusions.answer: εἰ + indicative ⇒ first class (assumed true) or second class (contrary to fact, with ἄν later). ἐάν + subjunctive ⇒ third class, a real maybe.
confusions.example: “εἰ συνηγέρθητε” (Col 3:1) · “ἐάν τις τηρήσῃ” (John 8:51).

confusions.question: ἡμεῖς or ὑμεῖς?
confusions.test: Look at the first letter, and say it.
confusions.answer: ὑ has the u of YOU — ὑμεῖς is you all. ἡ is us — ἡμεῖς is we.
confusions.example: ἡμεῖς = we · ὑμεῖς = you all.

confusions.question: He allowed it — middle or passive?
confusions.test: Is he letting it be done to himself, or consenting to what is being done?
confusions.answer: Middle: he puts himself under it, “let yourself be baptised”. Passive: he gives way to it, “be filled”. Close cousins — the form decides.
confusions.example: “βάπτισαι” (Acts 22:16, middle) · “πληροῦσθε” (Eph 5:18, passive).

confusions.question: μή plus a verb — prohibitory subjunctive, or imperative prohibition?
confusions.test: Look at what comes after the μή.
confusions.answer: μή + aorist subjunctive ⇒ prohibitory subjunctive. μή + imperative ⇒ prohibition. The form after the μή is the whole tell.
confusions.example: “μὴ νομίσητε” (Matt 5:17, aorist subj.) · “μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε” (1 John 2:15, pres. impv.).

confusions.question: A question — deliberative subjunctive or optative?
confusions.test: Is the question being asked, or being reported?
confusions.answer: Asked straight out, “should we …?” ⇒ subjunctive. Reported, “they asked what it might be” ⇒ optative.
confusions.example: “ἐπιμένωμεν;” (Rom 6:1) · “τίς εἴη ἡ παραβολή” (Luke 8:9).

confusions.question: An order — hortatory subjunctive or plain imperative?
confusions.test: Is the speaker inside the command?
confusions.answer: “Let us …”, speaker included ⇒ hortatory subjunctive. “Do this”, pointed at you ⇒ imperative.
confusions.example: “ἐργαζώμεθα” (Gal 6:10, let us) · “χαίρετε” (1 Thess 5:16, you).

confusions.question: Which class of conditional?
confusions.test: Look at the particle, then the mood of the verb.
confusions.answer: εἰ + indicative ⇒ 1st (true) or 2nd (contrary to fact, ἄν later). ἐάν + subjunctive ⇒ 3rd, a real maybe. εἰ + optative ⇒ 4th, remote.
confusions.example: Col 3:1 · John 5:46 · John 8:51 · 1 Pet 3:14.

confusions.question: Articular or anarthrous?
confusions.test: Is there a ὁ, ἡ or τό in front of it?
confusions.answer: There is ⇒ articular, the joint is in place. There is not ⇒ anarthrous, ἀν- plus ἄρθρον. The word only names what is there; what an absence means is the separate three-way question under Poof.
confusions.example: John 1:1 has both in one clause: ὁ λόγος articular, θεός anarthrous.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Grace, mercy, peace from God our Father" (1 Tim. 1:2) — all nominative, no verb, opening a letter.
extraQuiz.why: Opening material, tied to nothing. A headline, not a rope.

extraQuiz.prompt: "You call me Teacher and Lord" (John 13:13) — the titles are nominative where you expected accusative.
extraQuiz.why: A title being used as the name people call him. Badges don't decline.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Son of David, have mercy on us" (Matt. 9:27).
extraQuiz.why: He is being called out to, not described.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus" (Rom. 1:1) — two nominatives, no verb.
extraQuiz.why: δοῦλος renames Παῦλος. No verb, so no claim — just a label.

extraQuiz.prompt: "He is our peace" (Eph. 2:14).
extraQuiz.why: A verb with a nominative each side. αὐτός is a pronoun, so it is the subject; ἡ εἰρήνη is what is said about him.

extraQuiz.prompt: "The good seed — these are the sons of the kingdom" (Matt. 13:38).
extraQuiz.why: σπέρμα is left dangling, but οὗτοι picks it up. Hanging by a pronoun.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Fight the good fight" (1 Tim. 1:18).
extraQuiz.why: The object echoes the verb — the same root, even.

extraQuiz.prompt: "He gave his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).
extraQuiz.why: Two accusatives, and “as” slips between them: object + complement. Slip "as" between the two accusatives — "his life AS a ransom" — so it is the complement, not the person-and-thing double.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They were cut to the heart" (Acts 2:37) — an inner wound, not a surgical one.
extraQuiz.why: Put “with respect to” in front and the sense improves.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Going a little farther, he fell on the ground" (Mark 14:35).
extraQuiz.why: μικρόν answers “how far?” — MMR, one of three.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Being justified freely by his grace" (Rom. 3:24).
extraQuiz.why: δωρεάν answers “how?” — MMR, two of three.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They chose Stephen, a man full of faith" (Acts 6:5).
extraQuiz.why: ἄνδρα renames the object. Alias.

extraQuiz.prompt: An infinitive's subject — the one performing the infinitive's action.
extraQuiz.why: Finite verbs take a nominative subject. Infinitives take an accusative one.

extraQuiz.prompt: "and the Word was God" (John 1:1c) — which use is θεός?
extraQuiz.why: ὁ λόγος has the article and wins the pecking order, so θεός is the predicate. No article, and still definite.

extraQuiz.prompt: he got into one of the boats
extraQuiz.greek: ἐμβὰς δὲ εἰς ἓν *τῶν πλοίων* (Luke 5:3)
extraQuiz.english: he got into one of the boats
extraQuiz.why: The boats are the whole; the one boat is the slice.

extraQuiz.prompt: Remember Lot's wife
extraQuiz.greek: μνημονεύετε *τῆς γυναικὸς* Λώτ (Luke 17:32)
extraQuiz.english: Remember Lot's wife
extraQuiz.why: μνημονεύω is a verb of memory — sensation — so it takes its object in the genitive.

extraQuiz.prompt: the least … is greater than he
extraQuiz.greek: ὁ δὲ μικρότερος … μείζων *αὐτοῦ* ἐστιν (Matt 11:11)
extraQuiz.english: the least … is greater than he
extraQuiz.why: μείζων is a comparative, so the genitive beside it is the “than”.

extraQuiz.prompt: and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ Σίμων ὁ ζηλωτὴς καὶ Ἰούδας *Ἰακώβου* (Acts 1:13)
extraQuiz.english: and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James
extraQuiz.why: “Judas [son] of James.” The kin word is left out for you to supply.

extraQuiz.prompt: Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω (John 11:43) — the underlined Λάζαρε.
extraQuiz.why: He is being called by name. The vocative has exactly one use, and this is it.

extraQuiz.prompt: δὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ (John 9:24) — the underlined τῷ θεῷ.
extraQuiz.why: Glory is handed over, and God is who it goes to. PORT — T.

extraQuiz.prompt: κατακόπτων ἑαυτὸν λίθοις (Mark 5:5) — the underlined λίθοις.
extraQuiz.why: Stones are a tool with no will of their own. MAMA — M.

extraQuiz.prompt: εἰ δὲ πνεύματι ἄγεσθε (Gal 5:18) — the underlined πνεύματι.
extraQuiz.why: The Spirit chooses, so it is a personal agent. MAMA — A.

extraQuiz.prompt: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος (John 1:1) — why does θεός have no article?
extraQuiz.why: A definite predicate nominative in front of the copula usually drops it. Colwell drops.

extraQuiz.prompt: τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (Titus 2:13) — one article over both nouns.
extraQuiz.why: Singular, personal, non-proper, same case, joined by καί. Sharp joins them into one person.

extraQuiz.prompt: σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος (John 6:69) — the underlined ὁ ἅγιος.
extraQuiz.why: An adjective with the article and no noun to describe. It has become the noun. ASAP — S.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ἡ δὲ ἐλθοῦσα προσεκύνει *αὐτῷ* (Matt 15:25)
she came and knelt before him
extraQuiz.greek: ἡ δὲ ἐλθοῦσα προσεκύνει *αὐτῷ* (Matt 15:25)
extraQuiz.english: she came and knelt before him
extraQuiz.why: προσκυνέω is a verb of worshipping, and the chart lists worshipping. BEAD — D, devoted verbs.

extraQuiz.prompt:
καὶ εὐθὺς ἐπιγνοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς *τῷ πνεύματι* αὐτοῦ (Mark 2:8)
Jesus, knowing at once in his spirit
extraQuiz.greek: καὶ εὐθὺς ἐπιγνοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς *τῷ πνεύματι* αὐτοῦ (Mark 2:8)
extraQuiz.english: Jesus, knowing at once in his spirit
extraQuiz.why: A realm, not a room — the same construction as the chart's own sphere example in Mark 8:12. HIT — I.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων κρίμα *ἑαυτῷ* ἐσθίει (1 Cor 11:29)
he eats and drinks judgment on himself
extraQuiz.greek: ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων κρίμα *ἑαυτῷ* ἐσθίει (1 Cor 11:29)
extraQuiz.english: he eats and drinks judgment on himself
extraQuiz.why: Judgment to his own cost. Personal interest, the disadvantage side. PORT — P.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ἐγὼ … *ὕδατι* βαπτίζω ὑμᾶς (Luke 3:16)
